title: The wild elephant
hook: Devadatta sets the elephant Nalagiri loose; the Buddha meets it with metta and it kneels (Vinaya, Cullavagga 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patacara, who lost everyone and heard: sister, recover your mind. Your line was recover your mind. Did the long out-breath help? Day seventy-seven.

Someone you trusted turns on you. Not a stranger. Family. Anyone who has lived through that knows it has its own particular sting. Devadatta was the Buddha's cousin, and a monk in his own order. And over the years, the old texts say, he grew jealous, and then ambitious. He asked to be put in charge of the whole community. He was refused. After that, he tried to kill the Buddha. Once he hired men to ambush him. Once he rolled a boulder down a hillside, and a splinter of rock cut the Buddha's foot. And then, in the city of Rajagaha, he went to the royal stables, where a huge, fierce elephant named Nalagiri was kept.
screen: `WHEN FAMILY TURNS ON YOU.` → `DEVADATTA, THE JEALOUS COUSIN.` → `A FIERCE ELEPHANT NAMED NALAGIRI.`

segments.voice: Devadatta tells the elephant keepers: when the monk Gotama comes down this street on his alms round, let Nalagiri loose. The story says they gave the elephant strong drink first, to make him wilder. In the morning the Buddha walks into the street with his monks. And there's Nalagiri, trunk up, ears spread, tail stiff, charging. People scramble onto rooftops. The monks beg him to turn back. He tells them not to be afraid. And he does the thing this whole path keeps returning to. He meets the elephant with metta, loving-kindness, spreading goodwill toward the animal charging him. Not a trick. Not a weapon. Just a mind with no hatred in it, pointed at a creature full of rage. Nalagiri lowers his trunk. He slows. He comes up to the Buddha and stands still, and the Buddha strokes his forehead. The texts say the elephant took dust from the Buddha's feet onto his own head, and walked back to his stable, calm. In the paintings, he kneels. The Dhammapada has a line for this, in Max Müller's old translation: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule." Now look back at this week of hard stories. A killer on the forest road, and a monk who walked on. I have stopped; you stop. Angulimala, stoned in town, and blessing a birth. Kisa Gotami, carrying her son everywhere. The mustard seed, and no house untouched. Patacara, sister, recover your mind. And today, an elephant, kneeling. Every one of them is about meeting the worst with something steadier than it.
screen: `LET THE ELEPHANT LOOSE.` · `MET WITH METTA.` · `DUST FROM HIS FEET.` · `A WEEK OF HARD STORIES.` · then, large: `THE ELEPHANT KNEELS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: meet one flash of anger with calm, and rehearse it now. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind something that reliably makes you angry. A certain tone. A certain person. Feel the heat start, the trunk going up. Now, instead of charging back, breathe out slowly and send it goodwill, the way the Buddha did. May you be at ease. May you be free of this rage. Watch what happens to the heat. The bell holds the time.
The wild elephant. Nalagiri, set loose by Devadatta and met with loving-kindness, who lowered his trunk and walked home calm.
Your line: the elephant kneels. Today, when someone charges at you, in person or online, meet it with one slow breath and goodwill before you answer. Day seventy-seven.

howItsDone: The taming of Nalagiri is one of the most often painted and sculpted scenes of the Buddha's life, and Buddhists across traditions practice metta, loving-kindness meditation, as the quality he showed.

fork.reveal: he tells his monks not to fear and meets Nalagiri with metta. the elephant lowers its trunk, stands still, and is stroked on the forehead.

trapdoor: what you thought: a miracle about controlling animals.
what it means: rage met by a mind with no hatred in it, and the rage going out.
what a scholar hears: Vinaya, Cullavagga 7.3; Nalagiri's taming is among the 'eight great events' shown in Pala-period art; the kneeling is the artists' picture, the text says he lowered his trunk.

notes: Dhammapada 5 quoted from Max Müller (1881); please check the exact wording and dash against the SBE X text.
Devadatta's attempts (hired archers/assassins, the rock from Vulture Peak, Nalagiri) follow Cullavagga 7.3; the strong drink is in the Vinaya account. Confirm.
The elephant taking dust from the Buddha's feet onto his head: in Cullavagga 7.3; confirm. 'Kneels' is the index's carry and the common artistic image; the script distinguishes them.
